items.title: Recursive resolvers vs authoritative servers
items.body: An authoritative server holds the records for a zone and answers only for it. A recursive resolver (your ISP, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) walks from the root to the TLD to the authoritative servers on behalf of clients and caches every answer for its TTL.
items.question: Think: when you change a record, whose cache decides how long users still see the old value?
items.answer: The recursive resolvers that already cached it. The authoritative server changes instantly, but each resolver keeps serving the old answer until its cached TTL expires.

source.name: RFC 1034 - Domain Names: Concepts and Facilities

items.title: NXDOMAIN answers are cached too
items.body: Resolvers cache negative answers (NXDOMAIN and NODATA). The negative TTL is the lesser of the SOA record TTL and the SOA MINIMUM field, so querying a name before you create it can make it look missing for that long.

source.name: RFC 2308 - Negative Caching of DNS Queries

items.title: No CNAME at the zone apex
items.question: Why can you not put a CNAME on example.com itself, only on www.example.com?
items.answer: A CNAME must be the only record at its name, but the apex must also carry SOA and NS records, so a CNAME there is invalid. Providers work around it with ALIAS, ANAME, or CNAME flattening, which resolve the target server-side and return plain A/AAAA records.

source.name: RFC 1034 - Domain Names: Concepts and Facilities

items.title: Planning a low-downtime IP change
items.question: You are moving a site to a new server tomorrow. The A record has a TTL of 86400. How do you make the cutover fast?
items.answer: Lower the TTL to something like 300 at least one old TTL (24 hours) before the move, so caches pick up the short TTL. Then change the record, keep the old server serving (or proxying) until traffic drains, and raise the TTL again afterwards.

source.name: RFC 1035 - Domain Names: Implementation and Specification

items.title: DNS propagation is really cache expiry
items.question: A colleague says the new record needs 48 hours to propagate, but it already works on your phone and not on your laptop. What is actually happening?
items.answer: Nothing is pushed across the internet. Different resolvers (and OS or browser caches) cached the old answer at different times and each drops it when its TTL runs out. Querying the authoritative server directly with dig @ns1... shows the true current value.

source.name: RFC 1034 - Domain Names: Concepts and Facilities

items.title: DNS-based failover is slow
items.question: Your health-checked DNS failover uses a 60 second TTL, yet some clients hit the dead region for many minutes. Why, and what helps?
items.answer: Some resolvers and clients ignore or floor TTLs, and long-lived processes (JVMs, connection pools) cache the resolved IP or keep existing connections open. Keep TTLs short, make clients re-resolve and recycle connections, and use anycast or a load balancer for failover that must be fast.
